# HDR and colour management

Frame Job reads each source as what it is: iPhone HDR video, HDR10 files, wide-gamut footage and camera log. It converts each one into the project's working colour before any grade, key or blend touches it. A project works in **SDR** (Rec. 709, the default) or in **HDR (HLG)** (Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020). An HDR project exports an HLG master, an HDR10 file or an SDR version, and you can preview that SDR version at any time. This page covers telling Frame Job how a file was shot, choosing the project's dynamic range and its blending, and the depth and colour you get in exports and saved frames.

Grading itself (Light, Color, curves, looks and the scopes) is covered in [Colour grading](color-grading.md). The export sheet as a whole is covered in [Export](export.md).

## How sources are read

You don't need to set anything for most footage. Each frame is converted once, at the very start of the picture pipeline, into the project's working colour. The chroma key and every grade then see the converted picture.

| Source | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary Rec. 709 or untagged video, stills, recordings | Drawn as is | Lifted to HDR reference white (203 cd/m², HLG 75 %), so it looks the same as it does in SDR |
| HLG video (e.g. iPhone HDR) | Converted to Rec. 709 by Frame Job, highlights rolled off smoothly | Kept as HLG, highlights above white intact |
| PQ / HDR10 video or stills | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off at the file's own peak (see [HDR10 peak](#hdr10-peak)) | Real HDR: display light up to 1,000 cd/m², brighter highlights rolled off to fit |
| Wide-gamut SDR (BT.2020 or P3 primaries with an SDR transfer, sRGB included) | Converted to Rec. 709; colours outside Rec. 709 are eased toward their brightness and rolled off instead of clipped | Converted into BT.2020 and lifted |
| Camera log (set in the Media tab) | Converted to a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture | Converted to real HDR |

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

# core/CLAUDE.md — Rust core rules

Applies to everything under `core/`. Build commands and the FFI three-file
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§5 the schemas, §6 the op table, §7 the architecture,
§7.10 this module map in the spec's words; its `README.md` is the index). The long form of
each entry below — why the seam fell where it did — is
`designs/adr/core-file-history.md` (the full history of every cut, with its
line counts, is archived; see its "Original" line); this file is what
governs a module now.

## Module map

- `lib.rs` — module declarations and re-exports only. No implementation code.
- `model.rs` — the spec §5.2 SHAPE: the project, its clips, sources,
  actions, markers and nests (a track is `model_track.rs` and the media
  types `model_media.rs`, both re-exported), with
  the serde defaults that say what an absent key means. The struct field
  names ARE the JSON keys. Nothing else lives here but `CanvasOutput`
  (`Canvas.output`, `sdr` or `hlg`, written only when `hlg`, format 23, spec
  §11 HD-2).
- `model_canvas.rs` — `CanvasBlending` (`Canvas.blending`, `encoded` or
  `linear`, written only when `linear`, format 24, spec §11 GR-18, HD-16),
  re-exported by `model.rs`; the recipe canvas carries it only when linear.
- `model_track.rs` — a track (`Track`, spec §5.2's `tracks[]` and a nest's),
  moved out of `model.rs` whole (road map "audio" AP10's toll T1) and
  re-exported by it; the track vocabulary's new keys land here: format 35's
  `volume` (0…`TRACK_VOLUME_MAX`, 4, written only when not 1) and `pan`
  (−1…1, written only when not 0), spec §11 AU-102, and format 36's
  `compressor` and `limiter` (the clip's `model_audio.rs` types, after `pan`,
  written only when set), spec §11 AU-150.

  spec §5.2's `media[]`), moved out of `model.rs` whole (road map

  `model_audio.rs`'s), re-exported whole by `model.rs` so every

  never reorder. `Normal` is 0 with no `+1`, so a zeroed uniform block, an
  older recipe and a file with no `blend` key all render source-over.

## Rules

**Modules and size.** New feature area = new module with its own
`impl Project` block. Soft cap ~600 lines; needing a new `// ---- name --`
banner section is the signal to split. Every module keeps a `//!` doc;
numeric and algorithmic choices get prose "why" comments. **A file at the cap
gives something up BEFORE it takes anything on**: the cut is a PURE MOVE,
landed and gated alone, so the feature's diff is attributable; budget the cut
against the pessimistic number, because an estimate here has run about two
thirds of the truth. Over the cap today and known debt, not licence:
`edit.rs`, whose
standing exemption is that its module doc IS the op table's semantics half
(the cut there, if ever forced, is the `Op` enum into an `edit_ops.rs`, and
never in the same phase as a feature). The current list is `wc -l`; named
seams are in `designs/adr/core-file-history.md` "Named next cuts".

**Dependencies.** `serde` and `serde_json` (the JSON the FFI speaks),
`tiny_http` (the agent's socket), and `serde_path_to_error`, which is there
so a patch refusal names the path to what only the type can refuse (a
misspelt variant, a `null` a required field cannot take), where serde alone
names only the value. `graphic` (the path crate `../graphic`, road map
10's motion-graphics engine), named by `ffi_graphic.rs` alone. It enables
`serde_json`'s `preserve_order`, and a feature is unified across a path
dependency, so the core's `serde_json` has it too; `Cargo.toml` spells it
out. `svgtypes` 0.16.1 (usvg's own pin, already in the lock) for its
named-colour table only, so a stored name agrees with what usvg draws
(`model_color.rs`). `sha2` for the `.fjgraphic` manifest's checksums
(G-46; also `graphic_ffi.rs`'s revision oracle).

**One implementation per algorithm.** Before writing time math, find the
existing implementation and route through it. Shared constants have exactly
one home (`TIMESCALE` in `time.rs`; `RC_*` caps in `format.rs`; the
inspector's bounds in `props_check.rs`).

**Purity.** Every edit takes `&self` and returns a new value — internally
clone-then-mutate. An op that would change nothing returns
`Outcome::Identity`, never an identical copy: an identical copy registers a
phantom undo step in the app.

**Errors.** Every edit answers `Result<Outcome, String>` — three arms and
one tier, no error enum. `Outcome::Applied` = the new project;
`Outcome::Identity` = the op is valid and nothing needed to change;
`Outcome::Refused(String)` = a rule declined it, carrying the rule's OWN
sentence rather than a second one written at the call site; `Err(String)` =
invalid arguments, unknown ids, parse failures — lowercase messages naming
the offending value. A refusal is not an error tier: both middle arms leave
the project untouched and register no undo step. No input may panic. FFI
mapping (`ffi_edit.rs`): `Applied` → a new handle; `Identity` → NULL with
neither channel written; `Refused` → NULL with the sentence through
`reason_out`; `Err` → NULL with the message through `err_out`; caught panic
→ `"internal error: <what>"`. The two channels are never both written.

**Times.** Every tick value that reaches the model is snapped to the
document's frame grid before it is stored (`time::snap_to_frame`). Never
store a sub-frame time. Where a range check names the value, the check runs
on what the CALLER sent and the snap follows it, so a refusal never names a
number the door rounded to (`props_check.rs`, `edit_props.rs`'s
`snap_motion` / `snap_animation`). The one family that is deliberately NOT
on the grid is the audio ramps — `audio.fade_in` / `fade_out`, the duck's
and the compressor's attack and release — because they are envelope lengths
sampled at the audio rate, not positions in the picture, and quantising them
to a video frame would round a 10 ms attack to nothing. The other is a SHIFT
(spec §11 #42): an op that moves several clips — the ripples, `close_gap`,
`insert_time`, `move_clip` — moves them all by ONE delta so abutments stay
exact, and at a rate whose frame is not a whole number of ticks (7 fps) a
moved start may sit a tick off the grid; a canvas rate change re-snaps (D7-3).

**FFI exports.** Every export: `#[no_mangle] pub unsafe extern "C"`, a `///`
comment restating the header contract, a `/// # Safety` paragraph, NULL
tolerance first, narrow `unsafe {}` blocks. Route through the shared helpers
in `ffi_util.rs` — a freshly hand-rolled `catch_unwind` is a review flag.
Export names mirror the Rust method exactly.

**Format changes.** Any change to persisted project state bumps
`RC_FORMAT_VERSION` in `format.rs` **and** the `#define` in
`core/include/framejob_core.h`; the reader must keep accepting every prior
version; the writer enforces the reader's caps. A bump whose new fields all
carry a serde default needs no migrate step (versions 3 through 15 have none;
15's one step only renumbers the branch's 1015)
but still bumps, because unknown keys are ignored at every level by design
and an older build would otherwise open the file, drop the new fields on read
and write the loss back on the next save; a bump that changes a field's
SHAPE adds a step at the migration hook (`migrate_1_to_2`). Each bump gets a
`schema_vN.rs` test that opens the previous versions' fixtures and reads the
new keys' ORDER off the written text, since a parsed `Value` sorts them.
**Nothing that checks the version writes the current number as a
literal**, so a bump edits `format.rs` (and `format_history.rs`'s paragraph)
and the header and no test or proof:
- The "one past the current version, refused" tests in
  `core/tests/schema_v3.rs` and `core/tests/model_tests.rs` compute
  `RC_FORMAT_VERSION + 1` and assert the refusal's whole message with
  both numbers.
- `schema_v3.rs`'s `the_header_states_the_same_format_version_as_the_core`
  holds the header's `#define` to `format.rs`'s constant, so a bump that
  moves only one of them fails `make test`.
- The schema tests' and `model_tests.rs`'s `/version` assertions read
  `RC_FORMAT_VERSION`; `schema_v10.rs`'s byte-for-byte round trips rewrite
  the fixture's version line through its `current()` helper.
- The proof scripts (`tools/proof/*_proof.py`) read the HEADER's number
  through a `format_version()` helper. `phase9`'s "one past" fixture is
  `format_version() + 1`, and its every-version loop runs up to the current
  version. A proof that expected a literal would fail weeks later, in
  someone else's session, with nothing pointing at the bump.

A fixture's own version (`e2_proof.py`'s `VERSION = 8`, a
`schema_vN.rs`'s older files) is a literal on purpose. One claim still
moves with the schema rather than the number: when a bump appends a key to
the video object, `schema_v4.rs`'s text assertion about what follows
`obscure` fails in `make test` and names the new neighbour.

**Tests.** All tests are black-box in `core/tests/` (no `#[cfg(test)]` in
`src/`), exercised **through the FFI** wherever possible, and verified
against independently written oracles — never golden files. Shared helpers
live in `tests/common/` (`content` / `contents` — "the same clips, ids
aside" — is the one spelling of that comparison, used by `nest`'s identity
claim and `scope`'s oracle alike); new feature area = new test file. Every
new export gets at least one test plus inclusion in the null-safety sweep.
Finish Rust work with `cargo fmt` and a clean `make lint`.

</system-reminder>

1	# HDR and colour management
2	
3	Frame Job reads each source as what it is: iPhone HDR video, HDR10 files, wide-gamut footage and camera log. It converts each one into the project's working colour before any grade, key or blend touches it. A project works in **SDR** (Rec. 709, the default) or in **HDR (HLG)** (Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020). An HDR project exports an HLG master, an HDR10 file or an SDR version, and you can preview that SDR version at any time. This page covers telling Frame Job how a file was shot, choosing the project's dynamic range and its blending, and the depth and colour you get in exports and saved frames.
4	
5	Grading itself (Light, Color, curves, looks and the scopes) is covered in [Colour grading](color-grading.md). The export sheet as a whole is covered in [Export](export.md).
6	
7	## How sources are read
8	
9	You don't need to set anything for most footage. Each frame is converted once, at the very start of the picture pipeline, into the project's working colour. The chroma key and every grade then see the converted picture.
10	
11	| Source | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| Ordinary Rec. 709 or untagged video, stills, recordings | Drawn as is | Lifted to HDR reference white (203 cd/m², HLG 75 %), so it looks the same as it does in SDR |
14	| HLG video (e.g. iPhone HDR) | Converted to Rec. 709 by Frame Job, highlights rolled off smoothly | Kept as HLG, highlights above white intact |
15	| PQ / HDR10 video or stills | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off at the file's own peak (see [HDR10 peak](#hdr10-peak)) | Real HDR: display light up to 1,000 cd/m², brighter highlights rolled off to fit |
16	| Wide-gamut SDR (BT.2020 or P3 primaries with an SDR transfer, sRGB included) | Converted to Rec. 709; colours outside Rec. 709 are eased toward their brightness and rolled off instead of clipped | Converted into BT.2020 and lifted |
17	| Camera log (set in the Media tab) | Converted to a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture | Converted to real HDR |
18	| Text, captions, shapes, graphics, the background colour | Drawn as is | Lifted to HDR reference white with the SDR sources |
19	
20	The conversion is Frame Job's own. It works the same way in the preview, in every export, in rendered and saved frames, and in the timeline's filmstrip and the Media tab's thumbnails. Changing a file's Camera Log redraws its thumbnails. An HLG or PQ still's thumbnail appears once its converted tile is ready, a moment after import.
21	
22	**View ▸ Show Ungraded** (⌃⌘U) turns off the grades, but this source conversion stays on. The conversion is how the file is read, not part of the grade.
23	
24	## Camera log
25	
26	Log footage looks flat and grey until it is converted. The **Camera Log** section of the **Media** tab tells Frame Job which curve a video file was shot with. The section appears once the project has a video file.
27	
28	1. Open the **Media** tab in the inspector and click the file in the list.
29	2. Choose a curve from the **Log** popup.
30	
31	It is a setting on the *file*, so every clip of that file follows it, reversed clips included. It is one undo step, **Camera Log**. A line under the popup says what is set. It reads "Select a video in the list" when the selected row is not a video file, and the popup is disabled. The section's header shows the selected file's setting (its curve or LUT name), so you can read it with the section collapsed.
32	
33	Relinking a file (**Relink…**) keeps its Camera Log setting.
34	
35	### The Log popup
36	
37	| Item | Curve | Camera gamut |
38	|---|---|---|
39	| None | No conversion: shows the log picture as recorded | — |
40	| Apple Log | Apple Log | BT.2020 |
41	| Apple Log 2 | Apple Log | Apple Wide Gamut |
42	| S-Log3 / S-Gamut3.Cine | Sony S-Log3 | S-Gamut3.Cine |
43	| S-Log3 / S-Gamut3 | Sony S-Log3 | S-Gamut3 |
44	| V-Log / V-Gamut | Panasonic V-Log | V-Gamut |
45	| C-Log2 / Cinema Gamut | Canon Log 2 | Cinema Gamut |
46	| C-Log2 / BT.2020 | Canon Log 2 | BT.2020 |
47	| C-Log3 / Cinema Gamut | Canon Log 3 | Cinema Gamut |
48	| C-Log3 / BT.2020 | Canon Log 3 | BT.2020 |
49	| LUT: *name* | Each `.cube` LUT already in the project | — |
50	| Use LUT… | Choose a `.cube` file that converts this file's log to Rec. 709 | — |
51	
52	Each built-in curve follows its maker's published curve and gamut; Cinema Gamut's primaries come from the ACES project's Canon transform. Frame Job's display transform puts 18 % grey at 42 % and 90 % white at about 78 %. Highlights roll off smoothly up to about six stops over grey. In an HDR (HLG) project the same footage becomes real HDR, with 18 % grey at HLG 38 % and no roll-off.
53	
54	Whether a log file is stored in video range or full range is read from the file itself.
55	
56	### Detection on import
57	
58	An iPhone **Apple Log** or **Apple Log 2** file is recognised by its label when you import it, so it looks like normal video straight away. The line under the popup then adds "— from the file", for example "Apple Log — from the file". Sony, Panasonic and Canon files carry no label Frame Job can read, so choose their curve by hand. To see an Apple Log file's raw log picture, choose **None**.
59	
60	### Using your own LUT
61	
62	**Use LUT…** opens a file panel asking you to "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709." The LUT is added to the project's media list and becomes this file's conversion, all in one **Camera Log** step. Its output is taken as Rec. 709. Other files can then pick it from the popup as **LUT: *name***. If that LUT is already in the Media list, its entry is reused instead of a second one being added. A file that can't be read as a LUT shows an error.
63	
64	A LUT that is some file's Camera Log counts as used: **Unused only** hides it, and Remove asks first.
65	
66	If you remove that LUT from the Media list, the alert says how many files use it as their Camera Log, for example "the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it". **Remove and Clear Looks** removes it, and those files go back to no conversion.
67	
68	### Camera Log and looks
69	
70	Camera Log is applied before any look. If a clip's file is converted by Camera Log and you also give the clip a camera LUT as a look, the Look section warns: "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice." It is only a warning, because a creative LUT on top is legitimate. See [Colour grading](color-grading.md).
71	
72	*Agents:* `set_media_color` (`color` is `{log, gamut?}`, `{lut}` or `null`); `get_project`'s `media[].color` shows `detected: true` for a file set at import.
73	
74	## HDR10 peak
75	
76	A PQ (HDR10) file has its highlights roll off to white at the brightness its own metadata names. Import reads the peak from the file: MaxCLL first, then the mastering display's maximum. It looks in the file's sample description and, when that names none, in the video stream's own HDR10 metadata (HEVC SEI, or AV1 metadata), so files from ffmpeg, HandBrake or x265 are read too. A file that names no peak is treated as 1,000 cd/m².
77	
78	The **HDR10** section of the **Media** tab appears once the project has a PQ file. That can be a video, or a PQ still image (PNG, HEIF or AVIF). Click the file in the list to see and change its peak. The section's header shows the selected file's peak in cd/m² (for example "4,000 cd/m²"), so you can read it with the section collapsed.
79	
80	| Control | What it does |
81	|---|---|
82	| **Peak** | The peak in cd/m², 1 to 10,000, with quick values 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 10,000. Typing a value overrides the file's. |
83	| **Use File's** | Goes back to the peak the file's metadata names. It is available only while an override is set. |
84	
85	The line under the controls says where the peak came from:
86	
87	- "Mastered at 4,000 cd/m² (MaxCLL, from the file)": the file's own value.
88	- "No HDR10 metadata — 1,000 cd/m² assumed": the file names no peak.
89	- "Set by hand; the file says 1,000 cd/m² (mastering display)": an override.
90	- "Set by hand; the file has no HDR10 metadata": an override on a file with no metadata.
91	
92	Each change is one undo step, **PQ Peak**. Changing the peak keeps the file's Camera Log setting, and changing the Camera Log keeps the peak. When the selected row is not a PQ file, the section reads "Select a PQ file in the list" and its controls are disabled.
93	
94	*Agents:* `set_media_color` with `peak` (a whole number of cd/m², 1–10000; a PQ still takes `{peak}` alone). `color` replaces the Camera Log and the peak together, so send both to keep both; `color: null` clears both the Camera Log and a peak override, and the peak goes back to the file's own reading. `media[].color.pq` shows the file's own reading.
95	
96	## The project's dynamic range
97	
98	The **Document** tab's **Canvas** section has a **Dynamic Range** popup:
99	
100	| Item | What the project works in | Default |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| SDR | Rec. 709 | Yes |
103	| HDR (HLG) | Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 | |
104	
105	The Document tab's summary shows the choice in its **Colour** row: "SDR — Rec. 709" or "HDR — Rec. 2100 HLG". Switching is one undo step, **Dynamic Range**.
106	
107	In an HDR (HLG) project:
108	
109	- **HDR sources keep their range.** An iPhone HDR clip keeps its highlights above white, and PQ and camera-log footage become real HDR.
110	- **SDR material is lifted to HDR reference white.** That covers SDR video, stills, screen recordings, titles, captions, shapes, graphics, the background and shadow colours. White is fixed at 203 cd/m² (HLG 75 %), so SDR material looks as it did and HDR highlights rise above it. There is no setting for the reference white.
111	- **HDR stills.** A still labelled HLG or PQ is drawn in its own colour, as HDR. An iPhone HDR photo with a gain map (HEIC) shows its HDR highlights in an HLG project. An SDR project draws its ordinary picture. In the SDR version (Show SDR Version, JPEG frames, SDR-version exports) a gain-map photo is its HDR rendition toned down, not the photo's own SDR image.
112	- **Grades keep their settings.** Switching changes no clip and no grade value. The grade's maths uses BT.2020's weights in an HLG project.
113	- **The chroma key keeps keying the colour it was picked on.** A key on an HLG, PQ or camera-log source compares the colour an SDR project would show, so it cuts the same pixels after the switch, or very nearly: HLG footage over P3 or BT.709 primaries, PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m² and a key picked on a gain-map photo key close to, but not exactly, what they keyed before.
114	- **Qualifiers read the HLG signal.** An adjustment clip's qualifier ranges are measured on the HLG values, so re-pick them after switching.
115	- **A `.cube` look reads its values as Rec. 709.** The Look section warns: "This project is HDR (HLG): a .cube LUT reads its values as Rec. 709."
116	- **Frames are saved as HDR.** **File ▸ Save Frame…** (⌥⌘E) as PNG or HEIC writes a 16-bit PNG or a 10-bit HEIC labelled BT.2100 HLG. A JPEG writes the SDR version.
117	
118	*Agents:* `set_canvas` with `output` set to `"sdr"` or `"hlg"`.
119	
120	### Show SDR Version
121	
122	**View ▸ Show SDR Version** shows the preview as the project's SDR version: the picture that 8-bit formats, JPEG frames and the SDR-version export get. A tag reading "SDR Version" sits in the preview's top-left corner while it is on, after the Ungraded and Selection tags when those are on. The scopes read the SDR version while it is on (see [Scopes in an HDR project](#scopes-in-an-hdr-project)).
123	
124	- It is a checkmark toggle with no shortcut. It is always enabled.
125	- It belongs to the window. It reaches the preview and the Preview Window (**View ▸ Preview Window**, ⇧⌘P), never an export or a saved frame, and it is not remembered: a new window starts with it off.
126	- In an SDR project, the picture already is the SDR version, so no pixel changes, but the tag still shows.
127	
128	The SDR version brings the HLG master back to Rec. 709. Everything up to reference white comes back as it was, so a white title stays white (about 248 of 255). Only the highlights above reference white are rolled off.
129	
130	*Agents:* `render_frame` with `sdr_version: true` draws the same picture. The menu toggle itself never reaches the tool.
131	
132	### Scopes in an HDR project
133	
134	In an HLG project, **View ▸ Scopes** (⌃⌘W) reads the HLG signal:
135	
136	- The waveform and parade label their lines in cd/m²: 0, 10, 51, 203 and 1000 at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 %.
137	- The 75 % line, HDR reference white, is dashed. Titles and SDR material sit on it, and HDR highlights rise above it.
138	- Luma and the vectorscope use BT.2020's weights. The vectorscope's colour-bar targets and skin line are BT.2020's too.
139	- Each slot's caption reads "HLG · cd/m²" (waveform, parade) or "Rec. 2100 HLG" (vectorscope, histogram), where an SDR project's reads "Rec. 709 · encoded".
140	
141	The scopes measure the picture on screen. With **Show SDR Version** on, they read the SDR version exactly as they would in an SDR project. **Show Ungraded** keeps the HLG reading. For everything else about the scopes, see [Colour grading](color-grading.md).
142	
143	*Agents:* `render_frame`'s scope options. In an HLG project each scope's JSON adds `signal: "hlg"`, and the waveform, parade and histogram add a `scale` (ticks in cd/m², reference white at 75 %).
144	
145	## Blending: encoded or linear light
146	## Limits
147	
148	- **Log detection is Apple-only.** Only Apple Log and Apple Log 2 are recognised on import. S-Log3, V-Log and Canon Log must be chosen by hand.
149	- **One setting per file.** Camera Log and the HDR10 peak belong to the media file, not to a clip. Two clips of one file can't be read differently.
150	- **The HDR10 peak is read once, at import.** Relinking a PQ file does not read its peak again; set it by hand if the new file differs. Relinking keeps the file's Camera Log.
151	- **Camera Log needs a video file.** It is refused on an audio file, an image or a LUT. A PQ still takes only a peak.
152	- **A peak only on a PQ file.** Setting a peak on a file that isn't PQ is refused.
153	- **A camera LUT as a look over Camera Log converts twice.** The Look section only warns.
154	- **The chroma key after switching to HDR (HLG) is close, not exact,** on HLG footage with P3 or BT.709 primaries, on PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m² and on an HDR gain-map photo. Re-pick the key if an edge changes.
155	- **Some Canon files look too contrasty.** A non-ProRes Canon file flagged as video range that actually stores full-range codes looks too contrasty after C-Log2 or C-Log3 conversion.
156	- **Two settings are fixed.** There is no Dolby Vision output, and SDR reference white in an HDR project is fixed at 203 cd/m².
157	- **Wide-gamut SDR projects aren't offered.** An SDR project always works in Rec. 709.

161	/// The Camera Log popup's Use LUT… (spec §11 GR-16): a `.cube` chosen in a
162	/// sheet panel becomes the selected video file's input conversion — Import
163	/// LUT…'s panel and probe (`EditorViewController+Look.swift`), then ONE
164	/// grouped edit "Camera Log": `add_media` (a file already in the list is
165	/// the row it already has) and `set_media_color {lut}`. The agent's mirror is
166	/// `import_media` then `set_media_color`.
167	extension EditorViewController {
168	    @objc func useCameraLogLUT(_ sender: Any?) {
169	        guard let document = document, let window = view.window,
170	            let media = document.selectedMedia,
171	            document.project.snapshot.media(media)?.kind == .video
172	        else {
173	            NSSound.beep()
174	            return
175	        }
176	        let panel = NSOpenPanel()
177	        panel.allowsMultipleSelection = false
178	        panel.canChooseDirectories = false
179	        panel.allowedContentTypes = [MediaImporter.lutType]
180	        panel.message = "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709."
181	        panel.beginSheetModal(for: window) { response in
182	            guard response == .OK, let url = panel.url else { return }
183	            Self.useCameraLogLUT(from: url, into: document, media: media)
184	        }
185	    }
186	
187	    /// The probe, then the one grouped step; off-event, so grouped
188	    /// explicitly. A refused file is the document's error sheet.
189	    static func useCameraLogLUT(from url: URL, into document: ProjectDocument, media: UInt32) {
190	        MediaImporter.probe(url: url, mayAsk: true) { result in
191	            do {
192	                let descriptor = try result.get()
193	                guard let lut = try backgroundMedia(for: descriptor, in: document.project) else {
194	                    NSSound.beep()
195	                    return
196	                }
197	                // The media's PQ peak override is kept (spec §11 HD-12).
198	                let pq = document.project.snapshot.media(media)?.color?.pq
199	                document.performGroupedEdit(
200	                    "Camera Log",
201	                    [.addMedia(descriptor: descriptor),
202	                     .setMediaColor(media: media, color: MediaColor(lut: lut, pq: pq))])
203	            } catch {
204	                document.present(error)
205	            }
206	        }
207	    }
208	}

425	//! - **The op.** `set_media_color {media, color}` sets a video media's

428	//!   only the keys `log`, `gamut`, `lut`, `peak`, `detected` and `pq`, each
429	//!   through serde's own vocabulary. `detected` and `pq` are import's to
430	//!   write, so the op refuses them; what the op stores always has `detected:
431	//!   false`, and an absent `gamut` is stored as the curve's first
432	//!   ([`LogCurve::gamuts`]). `peak` is a PQ file's override (spec §11 HD-12):
433	//!   `color` replaces the Camera Log and the override together, import's
434	//!   reading (`pq.file`, `pq.from`) survives every op, and `null` clears
435	//!   both, keeping the reading.
436	//! - **The rules** ([`Project::check_media_color`]), each its own sentence:
437	//!   the media is a video file, or an image whose colour is a PQ still's

441	//!   [`PEAK_MIN`]–[`PEAK_MAX`] and `from` goes with `file`. The op answers
442	//!   them as refusals; `add_media` (whose descriptor may carry a detected
443	//!   `color`) and `validate` (a file) as errors, as they answer every other
444	//!   field. The op's own: a `peak` only on a PQ file and in range, an image
445	//!   taking only a `peak` alone, and an asked `color` with none of `log`,

503	/// [`PEAK_MIN`]–[`PEAK_MAX`], and `from` present exactly when `file` is.
504	fn check_pq(pq: PqColor) -> Result<(), String> {
505	    for (key, value) in [("file", pq.file), ("peak", pq.peak)] {
506	        if let Some(n) = value.filter(|n| !(PEAK_MIN..=PEAK_MAX).contains(n)) {

518	/// `color` read strictly: `None` for `null`, else the setting and `peak`, or
519	/// the `Err` naming what is wrong — not an object, an unknown key, a `peak`
520	/// that is not a whole number, or a value serde refuses (its own sentence,
521	/// naming the variants).
522	fn read_color(color: &Value) -> Result<Option<Asked>, String> {
523	    let fields = match color {
524	        Value::Null => return Ok(None),
525	        Value::Object(fields) => fields,
526	        other => {
527	            return Err(format!(
528	                "color must be a json object or null, not {}",
529	                describe(other)
530	            ))
531	        }
532	    };
533	    if let Some(key) = fields
534	        .keys()
535	        .find(|key| !COLOR_KEYS.contains(&key.as_str()))
536	    {
537	        return Err(format!("unknown key \"{key}\" in color"));
538	    }
539	    let peak = match fields.get("peak") {
540	        None => None,
541	        Some(value) => Some(value.as_i64().ok_or_else(|| {
542	            format!(
543	                "color.peak must be a whole number of cd/m², not {}",
544	                describe(value)
545	            )
546	        })?),
547	    };
548	    let mut setting = fields.clone();
549	    setting.remove("peak");
550	    serde_json::from_value(Value::Object(setting))
551	        .map(|color| Some(Asked { color, peak }))
552	        .map_err(|e| format!("color does not match the schema: {e}"))
553	}

165	///   over P3 or BT.709, whose working colour was matrixed in scene light.
166	/// - `.pq` — the source is PQ: the working colour back to display light (the
167	///   inverse OETF, BT.2100's OOTF γ 1.2, × 1000/203), then GR-15's PQ arm's
168	///   matrix, gamut lift and shoulder to max(peak, 203)/203. Exact up to 1,000
169	///   cd/m²; close above, where BT.2390's EETF is not undone.
170	/// - `.log` — the layer's media has a built-in Camera Log (spec §11 HD-20
171	///   (a), #324): the working colour back to scene light (the inverse OETF,
172	///   HD-13 (e)'s BT.2020 reflection × `logHLGExposure`), × `logExposure /
173	///   logHLGExposure`, then GR-16's SDR arm's matrix, gamut lift and shoulder
174	///   to `logWhite`. Exact where the HLG arm floored no channel and did not
175	///   clip (reflection ≤ 3.74).
176	/// - `.unlift` — every other layer (LUT media, SDR sources, drawn layers):
177	///   HD-13 (h)'s inverse lift, unchanged, exact for a LUT media's output,
178	///   which HD-3 lifted.
179	///
180	/// The shader's `keyReadSDR` and `hlgUnliftSDR` read it from

183	enum KeyReading: Equatable {
184	    case unlift, hlg, pq(peak: UInt32?), log

186	    /// `LayerUniforms.keyReading`: 0 the un-lift, 1 the HLG arm, 2 the
187	    /// camera-log arm, and for PQ minus the shoulder's white, max(peak,
188	    /// 203)/203 with 1,000 cd/m² when none is named — never above −1, so the
189	    /// shader tells the four apart.
190	    var uniform: Float {
191	        switch self {
192	        case .unlift: return 0
193	        case .hlg: return 1

199	    /// The SDR colour this reading takes a working HLG colour to, unclamped:
200	    /// the shader's `keyReadSDR` (and, for `.unlift`, `hlgUnliftSDR`).
201	    func sdr(_ hlg: SIMD3<Float>) -> SIMD3<Float> {
202	        let scene = SIMD3<Float>(
203	            InputConversions.hlgInverseOETF(hlg.x), InputConversions.hlgInverseOETF(hlg.y),
204	            InputConversions.hlgInverseOETF(hlg.z))
205	        let ys = simd_dot(scene, InputConversions.luma2020)
206	        let light: SIMD3<Float>
207	        let white: Float
208	        switch self {
209	        case .unlift:
210	            return InputConversions.unliftSDR(hlg)
211	        case .hlg:
212	            light = ys > 1e-6
213	                ? InputConversions.hlgGain * scene * pow(ys, InputConversions.hlgSystemGamma - 1)
214	                : .zero
215	            white = InputConversions.hlgWhite
216	        case .pq(let peak):
217	            let display = ys > 0
218	                ? scene * pow(ys, InputConversions.hlgNominalGamma - 1) : .zero
219	            light = display * (InputConversions.pqWhite / InputConversions.pqReferenceWhite)
220	            white = InputConversions.pqShoulderWhite(peak: peak)
221	        case .log:
222	            light = scene * (InputConversions.logExposure / InputConversions.logHLGExposure)
223	            white = InputConversions.logWhite
224	        }
225	        let linear = Self.shoulder(
226	            Self.gamutLift(InputConversions.toBT709(from: .bt2020) * light), white: white)
227	        let encode = 1 / InputConversions.displayGamma
228	        return SIMD3<Float>(
229	            pow(max(linear.x, 0), encode), pow(max(linear.y, 0), encode),
230	            pow(max(linear.z, 0), encode))
231	    }

233	    /// The eyedropper's stored key in an HLG project: a picked HLG colour
234	    /// read through `sdr`, each channel clamped to [0, 1], its alpha kept.
235	    /// `.unlift`'s is `InputConversions.unliftedPick` itself, so the probe's
236	    /// P6 and P12 read one function.
237	    func pick(_ color: RGBA) -> RGBA {
238	        if self == .unlift { return InputConversions.unliftedPick(color) }
239	        guard color.count >= 3 else { return color }
240	        let rgb = sdr(SIMD3<Float>(Float(color[0]), Float(color[1]), Float(color[2])))
241	        return [rgb.x, rgb.y, rgb.z].map { Double(min(max($0, 0), 1)) } + color.dropFirst(3)
242	    }

247	    /// built-in Camera Log `.log`, a LUT (and no conversion) `.unlift`.
248	    static func of(_ conversion: InputConversion?, peak: UInt32?) -> KeyReading {
249	        switch conversion {
250	        case .hlg: return .hlg
251	        case .pq: return .pq(peak: peak)
252	        case .log: return .log

261	    /// its track's labels (`ThumbnailInput(track:)`, await-free) with its
262	    /// effective PQ peak; every other media, or none at `url`, `.unlift`. Off
263	    /// the main thread: the track lookup reads the file.
264	    static func of(media: MediaSnapshot, url: URL?) -> KeyReading {
265	        guard let url else { return .unlift }
266	        switch media.kind {

268	            // By the file's colour space. Should Core Graphics refuse the
269	            // still's HDR bitmap at draw time, the layer falls back to the SDR
270	            // path and the shader reads `.unlift` against this pick: rare, and
271	            // a re-pick fixes it.
272	            return of(StillColor.conversion(at: url), peak: media.color?.pq?.effectivePeak)
273	        case .video:
274	            if let color = media.color, let chosen = InputConversion.choose(input: color) {
275	                return of(chosen, peak: nil)
276	            }
277	            let track = CompositionBuilder.firstTrack(of: AVURLAsset(url: url), mediaType: .video)

288	    /// The keyed clips' one reading: theirs when every one agrees, else (and
289	    /// for none) the un-lift.

291	        guard let first = readings.first, readings.allSatisfy({ $0 == first }) else {
292	            return .unlift

297	    /// GR-15's gamut lift (the shader's `inputLift`): a colour with a negative
298	    /// channel moves toward its BT.709 luminance until its lowest channel is 0.
299	    private static func gamutLift(_ l: SIMD3<Float>) -> SIMD3<Float> {
300	        let low = min(l.x, l.y, l.z)
301	        guard low < 0 else { return l }
302	        let y = simd_dot(l, SIMD3<Float>(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722))
303	        return y <= 0 ? .zero : y + (l - y) * (y / (y - low))
304	    }
305	
306	    /// GR-15's shoulder (the shader's `inputShoulder`) from
307	    /// `InputConversions.shoulderKnee`, reaching 1 at `white`.
308	    private static func shoulder(_ l: SIMD3<Float>, white: Float) -> SIMD3<Float> {
309	        let knee = InputConversions.shoulderKnee
310	        let m = max(l.x, l.y, l.z)
311	        guard m > knee else { return l }
312	        var s: Float = 1
313	        if m < white {
314	            let t = (m - knee) / (1 - knee)
315	            let tw = (white - knee) / (1 - knee)
316	            s = knee + (1 - knee) * t * (1 + t / (tw * tw)) / (1 + t)
317	        }
318	        return l * (s / m)
319	    }

1	# HDR and colour management
2	
3	Frame Job reads each source as what it is: iPhone HDR video, HDR10 files, wide-gamut footage and camera log. It converts each one into the project's working colour before any grade, key or blend touches it. A project works in **SDR** (Rec. 709, the default) or in **HDR (HLG)** (Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020). An HDR project exports an HLG master, an HDR10 file or an SDR version, and you can preview that SDR version at any time. This page covers telling Frame Job how a file was shot, choosing the project's dynamic range and its blending, and the depth and colour you get in exports and saved frames.
4	
5	Grading itself (Light, Color, curves, looks and the scopes) is covered in [Colour grading](color-grading.md). The export sheet as a whole is covered in [Export](export.md).
6	
7	## How sources are read
8	
9	You don't need to set anything for most footage. Each frame is converted once, at the very start of the picture pipeline, into the project's working colour. The chroma key and every grade then see the converted picture.
10	
11	| Source | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| Ordinary Rec. 709 or untagged video, stills, recordings | Drawn as is | Lifted to HDR reference white (203 cd/m², HLG 75 %), so it looks the same as it does in SDR |
14	| HLG video (e.g. iPhone HDR) | Converted to Rec. 709 by Frame Job, highlights rolled off smoothly | Kept as HLG, highlights above white intact |
15	| PQ / HDR10 video or stills | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off at the file's own peak (see [HDR10 peak](#hdr10-peak)) | Real HDR: display light up to 1,000 cd/m², brighter highlights rolled off to fit |
16	| Wide-gamut SDR (BT.2020 or P3 primaries with an SDR transfer, sRGB included) | Converted to Rec. 709; colours outside Rec. 709 are eased toward their brightness and rolled off instead of clipped | Converted into BT.2020 and lifted |
17	| Camera log (set in the Media tab) | Converted to a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture | Converted to real HDR |
18	| Text, captions, shapes, graphics, the background colour | Drawn as is | Lifted to HDR reference white with the SDR sources |
19	
20	The conversion is Frame Job's own. It works the same way in the preview, in every export, in rendered and saved frames, and in the timeline's filmstrip and the Media tab's thumbnails. Changing a file's Camera Log redraws its thumbnails. An HLG or PQ still's thumbnail appears once its converted tile is ready, a moment after import.
21	
22	**View ▸ Show Ungraded** (⌃⌘U) turns off the grades, but this source conversion stays on. The conversion is how the file is read, not part of the grade.
23	
24	## Camera log
25	
26	Log footage looks flat and grey until it is converted. The **Camera Log** section of the **Media** tab tells Frame Job which curve a video file was shot with. The section appears once the project has a video file.
27	
28	1. Open the **Media** tab in the inspector and click the file in the list.
29	2. Choose a curve from the **Log** popup.
30	
31	It is a setting on the *file*, so every clip of that file follows it, reversed clips included. It is one undo step, **Camera Log**. A line under the popup says what is set. It reads "Select a video in the list" when the selected row is not a video file, and the popup is disabled. The section's header shows the selected file's setting (its curve or LUT name), so you can read it with the section collapsed.
32	
33	Relinking a file (**Relink…**) keeps its Camera Log setting.
34	
35	### The Log popup
36	
37	| Item | Curve | Camera gamut |
38	|---|---|---|
39	| None | No conversion: shows the log picture as recorded | — |
40	| Apple Log | Apple Log | BT.2020 |
41	| Apple Log 2 | Apple Log | Apple Wide Gamut |
42	| S-Log3 / S-Gamut3.Cine | Sony S-Log3 | S-Gamut3.Cine |
43	| S-Log3 / S-Gamut3 | Sony S-Log3 | S-Gamut3 |
44	| V-Log / V-Gamut | Panasonic V-Log | V-Gamut |
45	| C-Log2 / Cinema Gamut | Canon Log 2 | Cinema Gamut |
46	| C-Log2 / BT.2020 | Canon Log 2 | BT.2020 |
47	| C-Log3 / Cinema Gamut | Canon Log 3 | Cinema Gamut |
48	| C-Log3 / BT.2020 | Canon Log 3 | BT.2020 |
49	| LUT: *name* | Each `.cube` LUT already in the project | — |
50	| Use LUT… | Choose a `.cube` file that converts this file's log to Rec. 709 | — |
51	
52	Each built-in curve follows its maker's published curve and gamut; Cinema Gamut's primaries come from the ACES project's Canon transform. Frame Job's display transform puts 18 % grey at 42 % and 90 % white at about 78 %. Highlights roll off smoothly up to about six stops over grey. In an HDR (HLG) project the same footage becomes real HDR, with 18 % grey at HLG 38 % and no roll-off.
53	
54	Whether a log file is stored in video range or full range is read from the file itself.
55	
56	### Detection on import
57	
58	An iPhone **Apple Log** or **Apple Log 2** file is recognised by its label when you import it, so it looks like normal video straight away. The line under the popup then adds "— from the file", for example "Apple Log — from the file". Sony, Panasonic and Canon files carry no label Frame Job can read, so choose their curve by hand. To see an Apple Log file's raw log picture, choose **None**.
59	
60	### Using your own LUT
61	
62	**Use LUT…** opens a file panel asking you to "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709." The LUT is added to the project's media list and becomes this file's conversion, all in one **Camera Log** step. Its output is taken as Rec. 709. Other files can then pick it from the popup as **LUT: *name***. If that LUT is already in the Media list, its entry is reused instead of a second one being added. A file that can't be read as a LUT shows an error.
63	
64	A LUT that is some file's Camera Log counts as used: **Unused only** hides it, and Remove asks first.
65	
66	If you remove that LUT from the Media list, the alert says how many files use it as their Camera Log, for example "the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it". **Remove and Clear Looks** removes it, and those files go back to no conversion.
67	
68	### Camera Log and looks
69	
70	Camera Log is applied before any look. If a clip's file is converted by Camera Log and you also give the clip a camera LUT as a look, the Look section warns: "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice." It is only a warning, because a creative LUT on top is legitimate. See [Colour grading](color-grading.md).
71	
72	*Agents:* `set_media_color` (`color` is `{log, gamut?}`, `{lut}` or `null`); `get_project`'s `media[].color` shows `detected: true` for a file set at import.
73	
74	## HDR10 peak
75	
76	A PQ (HDR10) file has its highlights roll off to white at the brightness its own metadata names. Import reads the peak from the file: MaxCLL first, then the mastering display's maximum. It looks in the file's sample description and, when that names none, in the video stream's own HDR10 metadata (HEVC SEI, or AV1 metadata), so files from ffmpeg, HandBrake or x265 are read too. A file that names no peak is treated as 1,000 cd/m².
77	
78	The **HDR10** section of the **Media** tab appears once the project has a PQ file. That can be a video, or a PQ still image (PNG, HEIF or AVIF). Click the file in the list to see and change its peak. The section's header shows the selected file's peak in cd/m² (for example "4,000 cd/m²"), so you can read it with the section collapsed.
79	
80	| Control | What it does |
81	|---|---|
82	| **Peak** | The peak in cd/m², 1 to 10,000, with quick values 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 10,000. Typing a value overrides the file's. |
83	| **Use File's** | Goes back to the peak the file's metadata names. It is available only while an override is set. |
84	
85	The line under the controls says where the peak came from:
86	
87	- "Mastered at 4,000 cd/m² (MaxCLL, from the file)": the file's own value.
88	- "No HDR10 metadata — 1,000 cd/m² assumed": the file names no peak.
89	- "Set by hand; the file says 1,000 cd/m² (mastering display)": an override.
90	- "Set by hand; the file has no HDR10 metadata": an override on a file with no metadata.
91	
92	Each change is one undo step, **PQ Peak**. Changing the peak keeps the file's Camera Log setting, and changing the Camera Log keeps the peak. When the selected row is not a PQ file, the section reads "Select a PQ file in the list" and its controls are disabled.
93	
94	*Agents:* `set_media_color` with `peak` (a whole number of cd/m², 1–10000; a PQ still takes `{peak}` alone). `color` replaces the Camera Log and the peak together, so send both to keep both; `color: null` clears both the Camera Log and a peak override, and the peak goes back to the file's own reading. `media[].color.pq` shows the file's own reading.
95	
96	## The project's dynamic range
97	
98	The **Document** tab's **Canvas** section has a **Dynamic Range** popup:
99	
100	| Item | What the project works in | Default |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| SDR | Rec. 709 | Yes |
103	| HDR (HLG) | Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 | |
104	
105	The Document tab's summary shows the choice in its **Colour** row: "SDR — Rec. 709" or "HDR — Rec. 2100 HLG". Switching is one undo step, **Dynamic Range**.
106	
107	In an HDR (HLG) project:
108	
109	- **HDR sources keep their range.** An iPhone HDR clip keeps its highlights above white, and PQ and camera-log footage become real HDR.
110	- **SDR material is lifted to HDR reference white.** That covers SDR video, stills, screen recordings, titles, captions, shapes, graphics, the background and shadow colours. White is fixed at 203 cd/m² (HLG 75 %), so SDR material looks as it did and HDR highlights rise above it. There is no setting for the reference white.
111	- **HDR stills.** A still labelled HLG or PQ is drawn in its own colour, as HDR. An iPhone HDR photo with a gain map (HEIC) shows its HDR highlights in an HLG project. An SDR project draws its ordinary picture. In the SDR version (Show SDR Version, JPEG frames, SDR-version exports) a gain-map photo is its HDR rendition toned down, not the photo's own SDR image.
112	- **Grades keep their settings.** Switching changes no clip and no grade value. The grade's maths uses BT.2020's weights in an HLG project.
113	- **The chroma key keeps keying the colour it was picked on.** A key on an HLG, PQ or camera-log source compares the colour an SDR project would show, so it cuts the same pixels after the switch, or very nearly: HLG footage over P3 or BT.709 primaries, PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m² and a key picked on a gain-map photo key close to, but not exactly, what they keyed before.
114	- **Qualifiers read the HLG signal.** An adjustment clip's qualifier ranges are measured on the HLG values, so re-pick them after switching.
115	- **A `.cube` look reads its values as Rec. 709.** The Look section warns: "This project is HDR (HLG): a .cube LUT reads its values as Rec. 709."
116	- **Frames are saved as HDR.** **File ▸ Save Frame…** (⌥⌘E) as PNG or HEIC writes a 16-bit PNG or a 10-bit HEIC labelled BT.2100 HLG. A JPEG writes the SDR version.
117	
118	*Agents:* `set_canvas` with `output` set to `"sdr"` or `"hlg"`.
119	
120	### Show SDR Version
121	
122	**View ▸ Show SDR Version** shows the preview as the project's SDR version: the picture that 8-bit formats, JPEG frames and the SDR-version export get. A tag reading "SDR Version" sits in the preview's top-left corner while it is on, after the Ungraded and Selection tags when those are on. The scopes read the SDR version while it is on (see [Scopes in an HDR project](#scopes-in-an-hdr-project)).
123	
124	- It is a checkmark toggle with no shortcut. It is always enabled.
125	- It belongs to the window. It reaches the preview and the Preview Window (**View ▸ Preview Window**, ⇧⌘P), never an export or a saved frame, and it is not remembered: a new window starts with it off.
126	- In an SDR project, the picture already is the SDR version, so no pixel changes, but the tag still shows.
127	
128	The SDR version brings the HLG master back to Rec. 709. Everything up to reference white comes back as it was, so a white title stays white (about 248 of 255). Only the highlights above reference white are rolled off.
129	
130	*Agents:* `render_frame` with `sdr_version: true` draws the same picture. The menu toggle itself never reaches the tool.
131	
132	### Scopes in an HDR project
133	
134	In an HLG project, **View ▸ Scopes** (⌃⌘W) reads the HLG signal:
135	
136	- The waveform and parade label their lines in cd/m²: 0, 10, 51, 203 and 1000 at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 %.
137	- The 75 % line, HDR reference white, is dashed. Titles and SDR material sit on it, and HDR highlights rise above it.
138	- Luma and the vectorscope use BT.2020's weights. The vectorscope's colour-bar targets and skin line are BT.2020's too.
139	- Each slot's caption reads "HLG · cd/m²" (waveform, parade) or "Rec. 2100 HLG" (vectorscope, histogram), where an SDR project's reads "Rec. 709 · encoded".
140	
141	The scopes measure the picture on screen. With **Show SDR Version** on, they read the SDR version exactly as they would in an SDR project. **Show Ungraded** keeps the HLG reading. For everything else about the scopes, see [Colour grading](color-grading.md).
142	
143	*Agents:* `render_frame`'s scope options. In an HLG project each scope's JSON adds `signal: "hlg"`, and the waveform, parade and histogram add a `scale` (ticks in cd/m², reference white at 75 %).
144	
145	## Blending: encoded or linear light
146	## Limits
147	
148	- **Log detection is Apple-only.** Only Apple Log and Apple Log 2 are recognised on import. S-Log3, V-Log and Canon Log must be chosen by hand.
149	- **One setting per file.** Camera Log and the HDR10 peak belong to the media file, not to a clip. Two clips of one file can't be read differently.
150	- **The HDR10 peak is read once, at import.** Relinking a PQ file does not read its peak again; set it by hand if the new file differs. Relinking keeps the file's Camera Log.
151	- **Camera Log needs a video file.** It is refused on an audio file, an image or a LUT. A PQ still takes only a peak.
152	- **A peak only on a PQ file.** Setting a peak on a file that isn't PQ is refused.
153	- **A camera LUT as a look over Camera Log converts twice.** The Look section only warns.
154	- **The chroma key after switching to HDR (HLG) is close, not exact,** on HLG footage with P3 or BT.709 primaries, on PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m² and on an HDR gain-map photo. Re-pick the key if an edge changes.
155	- **Some Canon files look too contrasty.** A non-ProRes Canon file flagged as video range that actually stores full-range codes looks too contrasty after C-Log2 or C-Log3 conversion.
156	- **Two settings are fixed.** There is no Dolby Vision output, and SDR reference white in an HDR project is fixed at 203 cd/m².
157	- **Wide-gamut SDR projects aren't offered.** An SDR project always works in Rec. 709.

161	/// The Camera Log popup's Use LUT… (spec §11 GR-16): a `.cube` chosen in a
162	/// sheet panel becomes the selected video file's input conversion — Import
163	/// LUT…'s panel and probe (`EditorViewController+Look.swift`), then ONE
164	/// grouped edit "Camera Log": `add_media` (a file already in the list is
165	/// the row it already has) and `set_media_color {lut}`. The agent's mirror is
166	/// `import_media` then `set_media_color`.
167	extension EditorViewController {
168	    @objc func useCameraLogLUT(_ sender: Any?) {
169	        guard let document = document, let window = view.window,
170	            let media = document.selectedMedia,
171	            document.project.snapshot.media(media)?.kind == .video
172	        else {
173	            NSSound.beep()
174	            return
175	        }
176	        let panel = NSOpenPanel()
177	        panel.allowsMultipleSelection = false
178	        panel.canChooseDirectories = false
179	        panel.allowedContentTypes = [MediaImporter.lutType]
180	        panel.message = "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709."
181	        panel.beginSheetModal(for: window) { response in
182	            guard response == .OK, let url = panel.url else { return }
183	            Self.useCameraLogLUT(from: url, into: document, media: media)
184	        }
185	    }
186	
187	    /// The probe, then the one grouped step; off-event, so grouped
188	    /// explicitly. A refused file is the document's error sheet.
189	    static func useCameraLogLUT(from url: URL, into document: ProjectDocument, media: UInt32) {
190	        MediaImporter.probe(url: url, mayAsk: true) { result in
191	            do {
192	                let descriptor = try result.get()
193	                guard let lut = try backgroundMedia(for: descriptor, in: document.project) else {
194	                    NSSound.beep()
195	                    return
196	                }
197	                // The media's PQ peak override is kept (spec §11 HD-12).
198	                let pq = document.project.snapshot.media(media)?.color?.pq
199	                document.performGroupedEdit(
200	                    "Camera Log",
201	                    [.addMedia(descriptor: descriptor),
202	                     .setMediaColor(media: media, color: MediaColor(lut: lut, pq: pq))])
203	            } catch {
204	                document.present(error)
205	            }
206	        }
207	    }
208	}

221	    /// with each gamut it pairs with.
222	    static let curves: [CameraLogChoice] = [
223	        .curve(.appleLog, .bt2020), .curve(.appleLog2, .appleWideGamut),

232	        if let log = color?.log, let gamut = color?.effectiveGamut {
233	            self = .curve(log, gamut)
234	        } else if let lut = color?.lut {
235	            self = .lut(lut)
236	        } else {

244	        switch self {

522	fn read_color(color: &Value) -> Result<Option<Asked>, String> {

158	/// How an HLG project's chroma key reads a keyed layer (spec §11 HD-19 (c),
159	/// #312, the owner's "Key means SDR colour"): the colour it compares against
160	/// the stored key is the one an SDR project shows for that pixel, so a key
161	/// picked in an SDR project keys the same colour after the switch to HLG.
162	///
163	/// - `.hlg` — the layer's source is HLG: GR-15's HLG arm over BT.2020, applied
164	///   to the working colour. Exact for an HLG BT.2020 source; close for HLG
165	///   over P3 or BT.709, whose working colour was matrixed in scene light.
166	/// - `.pq` — the source is PQ: the working colour back to display light (the
167	///   inverse OETF, BT.2100's OOTF γ 1.2, × 1000/203), then GR-15's PQ arm's
168	///   matrix, gamut lift and shoulder to max(peak, 203)/203. Exact up to 1,000
169	///   cd/m²; close above, where BT.2390's EETF is not undone.
170	/// - `.log` — the layer's media has a built-in Camera Log (spec §11 HD-20
171	///   (a), #324): the working colour back to scene light (the inverse OETF,
172	///   HD-13 (e)'s BT.2020 reflection × `logHLGExposure`), × `logExposure /
173	///   logHLGExposure`, then GR-16's SDR arm's matrix, gamut lift and shoulder
174	///   to `logWhite`. Exact where the HLG arm floored no channel and did not
175	///   clip (reflection ≤ 3.74).
176	/// - `.unlift` — every other layer (LUT media, SDR sources, drawn layers):
177	///   HD-13 (h)'s inverse lift, unchanged, exact for a LUT media's output,
178	///   which HD-3 lifted.
179	///

181	/// `LayerUniforms.keyReading` (`uniform`); `sdr` is their CPU twin, and the
182	/// HLG eyedropper stores `pick` of the clicked colour.
183	enum KeyReading: Equatable {
184	    case unlift, hlg, pq(peak: UInt32?), log
185	
186	    /// `LayerUniforms.keyReading`: 0 the un-lift, 1 the HLG arm, 2 the
187	    /// camera-log arm, and for PQ minus the shoulder's white, max(peak,
188	    /// 203)/203 with 1,000 cd/m² when none is named — never above −1, so the
189	    /// shader tells the four apart.
190	    var uniform: Float {
191	        switch self {
192	        case .unlift: return 0
193	        case .hlg: return 1
194	        case .log: return 2
195	        case .pq(let peak): return -InputConversions.pqShoulderWhite(peak: peak)
196	        }
197	    }

199	    /// The SDR colour this reading takes a working HLG colour to, unclamped:
200	    /// the shader's `keyReadSDR` (and, for `.unlift`, `hlgUnliftSDR`).
201	    func sdr(_ hlg: SIMD3<Float>) -> SIMD3<Float> {
202	        let scene = SIMD3<Float>(
203	            InputConversions.hlgInverseOETF(hlg.x), InputConversions.hlgInverseOETF(hlg.y),
204	            InputConversions.hlgInverseOETF(hlg.z))
205	        let ys = simd_dot(scene, InputConversions.luma2020)
206	        let light: SIMD3<Float>
207	        let white: Float
208	        switch self {
209	        case .unlift:
210	            return InputConversions.unliftSDR(hlg)
211	        case .hlg:
212	            light = ys > 1e-6
213	                ? InputConversions.hlgGain * scene * pow(ys, InputConversions.hlgSystemGamma - 1)
214	                : .zero
215	            white = InputConversions.hlgWhite
216	        case .pq(let peak):
217	            let display = ys > 0
218	                ? scene * pow(ys, InputConversions.hlgNominalGamma - 1) : .zero
219	            light = display * (InputConversions.pqWhite / InputConversions.pqReferenceWhite)
220	            white = InputConversions.pqShoulderWhite(peak: peak)
221	        case .log:
222	            light = scene * (InputConversions.logExposure / InputConversions.logHLGExposure)
223	            white = InputConversions.logWhite
224	        }
225	        let linear = Self.shoulder(
226	            Self.gamutLift(InputConversions.toBT709(from: .bt2020) * light), white: white)
227	        let encode = 1 / InputConversions.displayGamma
228	        return SIMD3<Float>(
229	            pow(max(linear.x, 0), encode), pow(max(linear.y, 0), encode),
230	            pow(max(linear.z, 0), encode))
231	    }

233	    /// The eyedropper's stored key in an HLG project: a picked HLG colour
234	    /// read through `sdr`, each channel clamped to [0, 1], its alpha kept.
235	    /// `.unlift`'s is `InputConversions.unliftedPick` itself, so the probe's
236	    /// P6 and P12 read one function.
237	    func pick(_ color: RGBA) -> RGBA {
238	        if self == .unlift { return InputConversions.unliftedPick(color) }
239	        guard color.count >= 3 else { return color }
240	        let rgb = sdr(SIMD3<Float>(Float(color[0]), Float(color[1]), Float(color[2])))
241	        return [rgb.x, rgb.y, rgb.z].map { Double(min(max($0, 0), 1)) } + color.dropFirst(3)
242	    }

244	    /// The reading of a source whose SDR-project step-0 choice is
245	    /// `conversion` — a frame's `choose(input:buffer:output: .sdr)` or a
246	    /// still's `StillColor` arm — with its media's effective PQ peak: a
247	    /// built-in Camera Log `.log`, a LUT (and no conversion) `.unlift`.
248	    static func of(_ conversion: InputConversion?, peak: UInt32?) -> KeyReading {
249	        switch conversion {
250	        case .hlg: return .hlg
251	        case .pq: return .pq(peak: peak)
252	        case .log: return .log
253	        default: return .unlift
254	        }
255	    }

257	    /// The reading of a media, for the eyedropper, which has no frame: a
258	    /// still by its colour space with its effective PQ peak (spec §11 HD-20
259	    /// (b)); a video by its Camera Log when one converts it (GR-16 chooses
260	    /// before the labels: a built-in curve `.log`, a LUT `.unlift`), else by
261	    /// its track's labels (`ThumbnailInput(track:)`, await-free) with its
262	    /// effective PQ peak; every other media, or none at `url`, `.unlift`. Off
263	    /// the main thread: the track lookup reads the file.
264	    static func of(media: MediaSnapshot, url: URL?) -> KeyReading {
265	        guard let url else { return .unlift }
266	        switch media.kind {
267	        case .image:
268	            // By the file's colour space. Should Core Graphics refuse the
269	            // still's HDR bitmap at draw time, the layer falls back to the SDR
270	            // path and the shader reads `.unlift` against this pick: rare, and
271	            // a re-pick fixes it.
272	            return of(StillColor.conversion(at: url), peak: media.color?.pq?.effectivePeak)
273	        case .video:
274	            if let color = media.color, let chosen = InputConversion.choose(input: color) {
275	                return of(chosen, peak: nil)
276	            }
277	            let track = CompositionBuilder.firstTrack(of: AVURLAsset(url: url), mediaType: .video)
278	            switch track.flatMap(ThumbnailInput.init(track:))?.transfer {
279	            case .hlg: return .hlg
280	            case .pq: return .pq(peak: media.color?.pq?.effectivePeak)

288	    /// The keyed clips' one reading: theirs when every one agrees, else (and
289	    /// for none) the un-lift.
290	    static func common(_ readings: [KeyReading]) -> KeyReading {
291	        guard let first = readings.first, readings.allSatisfy({ $0 == first }) else {
292	            return .unlift

295	    }

297	    /// GR-15's gamut lift (the shader's `inputLift`): a colour with a negative
298	    /// channel moves toward its BT.709 luminance until its lowest channel is 0.
299	    private static func gamutLift(_ l: SIMD3<Float>) -> SIMD3<Float> {
300	        let low = min(l.x, l.y, l.z)
301	        guard low < 0 else { return l }
302	        let y = simd_dot(l, SIMD3<Float>(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722))
303	        return y <= 0 ? .zero : y + (l - y) * (y / (y - low))
304	    }
305	
306	    /// GR-15's shoulder (the shader's `inputShoulder`) from
307	    /// `InputConversions.shoulderKnee`, reaching 1 at `white`.
308	    private static func shoulder(_ l: SIMD3<Float>, white: Float) -> SIMD3<Float> {
309	        let knee = InputConversions.shoulderKnee
310	        let m = max(l.x, l.y, l.z)
311	        guard m > knee else { return l }
312	        var s: Float = 1
313	        if m < white {
314	            let t = (m - knee) / (1 - knee)
315	            let tw = (white - knee) / (1 - knee)
316	            s = knee + (1 - knee) * t * (1 + t / (tw * tw)) / (1 + t)
317	        }
318	        return l * (s / m)
319	    }
320	}

---
title: "Camera log from your own LUT"
description: "Convert a log file with a .cube LUT instead of a built-in curve, share that LUT between files, and remove it without surprises."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

When [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) has no built-in curve for your footage, a `.cube` LUT can do the conversion instead. You pick the LUT once, and every clip of that file comes out as normal-looking video.

<AtAGlance
  where={['Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log ▸ Use LUT…', 'Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log ▸ LUT: name']}
  tools={['import_media', 'set_media_color', 'remove_media']}
/>

## Use LUT…

<Steps>

1. Open the **Media** tab and click the video file in the list.

2. In the **Camera Log** section, choose **Use LUT…** from the **Log** popup.

3. Pick the `.cube` file. The panel asks you to "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709."

</Steps>

The LUT joins the project's media list and becomes this file's conversion, all as one undo step called **Camera Log**. The line under the popup and the section's header then read **LUT: name**.

Frame Job takes the LUT's output as Rec. 709, so use a LUT made for that job. Like every Camera Log setting, it belongs to the file: every clip of the file follows it, reversed clips included, and it's applied before the chroma key and every grade.

A file takes a curve or a LUT, not both, so choosing one replaces the other. A PQ file keeps its [peak override](/hdr/hdr10-peak/#undo-and-camera-log).

If the file you pick is already in the Media list, Frame Job uses that entry and doesn't add a second one.

The LUT has to be a 3D `.cube` of size 2 to 65 with the default 0 to 1 domain, and no larger than 32 MiB. Anything else shows an error naming the file and what's wrong with it, and nothing changes. For example: "“Film.cube” is not a LUT Frame Job reads: line 2: LUT_3D_SIZE 200 is outside 2–65." [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/) has the format in full.

## A LUT already in the project

Every `.cube` LUT in the project is listed in the **Log** popup as **LUT: name**, between the built-in curves and **Use LUT…**. The name is the file's name without `.cube`.

To use the same LUT on another file, click that file in the list and choose its row. One LUT can convert any number of files.

The popup and the [Look section](/color/looks/) read the same media list. A LUT you imported as a look is offered here, and a LUT you added with **Use LUT…** appears in the Look section's Imported group.

To take a LUT off one file, choose **None** or a curve in the **Log** popup. The LUT stays in the Media list.

## A LUT in use

A LUT that is some file's Camera Log counts as used, even when no clip has it as a look. **Unused only** hides it from the [Media list](/projects/media-tab/#unused-only), and Remove asks first.

## Remove the LUT

Right-click the LUT's row on the Media tab and choose **Remove**. The alert says what depends on it, for example:

- "It is the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it."
- "It is the look of 1 clip, which keeps its place and loses the look. …and the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it."

**Remove and Clear Looks** removes the LUT as one undo step, **Remove Media**. Those files go back to no conversion, so they show the log picture as recorded. Clips that had it as a look stay where they are and lose the look. A PQ file keeps its peak. **Cancel** changes nothing.

The `.cube` file on your disk is never touched. See [Remove media](/projects/remove-media/).

## Camera Log and looks

Camera Log is applied before any look, so a look works on the picture the conversion made.

If a clip's look is a `.cube` LUT and its file has a Camera Log, the Look section warns: "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice."

It's only a warning, and Frame Job changes nothing, because a creative LUT on top of a conversion is fine. If the look really is a camera LUT, keep it in one place: either in the **Log** popup or as the clip's look, not both.

The eight built-in looks never show this warning. A `.cube` look on a PQ (HDR10) file does show it, even with **Log** set to **None**.

## Good to know

- In an HDR (HLG) project, a LUT's output is treated as SDR and [lifted to reference white](/hdr/dynamic-range/#sdr-material-in-an-hdr-project), so the file gains no HDR highlights. A built-in curve does become real HDR there.
- If the LUT can't be found or drawn, the footage shows unconverted, as flat log, until you [relink](/projects/relink-media/) the LUT. A LUT relinks like any other file in the Media list.
- Relinking the video file keeps its Camera Log.
- Camera Log is for video files. With an audio file, an image or a LUT selected, the popup is disabled and the line reads "Select a video in the list".
- **View ▸ Show Ungraded** turns looks and grades off and leaves the conversion on, because the conversion is how the file is read.

## With an agent

An agent takes two steps where a person takes one: `import_media` brings the `.cube` into the project, then `set_media_color` names it as the file's conversion. See [Tools: media](/mcp/tools-media/).

## Related

- [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/)
- [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/)
- [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/)
- [The Media tab](/projects/media-tab/)

---
title: "HDR10 peak"
description: "See the peak brightness Frame Job read from a PQ file, override it when the metadata is wrong or missing, and go back to the file's own value."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A PQ (HDR10) file's highlights roll off to white at the brightness its own metadata names. Frame Job reads that peak when you import the file, and the **HDR10** section lets you see it and change it when the metadata is wrong or missing.

<AtAGlance
  where="Media tab ▸ HDR10"
  tools={['set_media_color', 'get_project']}
/>

## The peak a file names

Import reads the peak by itself, so most files need nothing from you. It takes MaxCLL first, when that's present and not zero, then the mastering display's maximum.

| The file is | Frame Job looks in |
| --- | --- |
| A video | The file's sample description. When that names no peak, the video stream's own HDR10 metadata (HEVC SEI or AV1 metadata), so files from ffmpeg, HandBrake or x265 are read too. |
| A PNG still | Its `cLLI` and `mDCV` chunks. |
| A HEIF or AVIF still | The `clli` and `mdcv` boxes of its main image. |

A file that names no peak is still read as PQ, and it's treated as 1,000 cd/m².

What the peak does depends on the [project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/):

- **In an SDR project**, highlights roll off smoothly to white at the peak. A peak below 203 cd/m², HDR reference white, counts as 203.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project**, the picture keeps display light up to 1,000 cd/m². A peak above that rolls brighter highlights off to fit, and a lower peak doesn't change the picture.

## The HDR10 section

The **HDR10** section of the **Media** tab appears once the project has a PQ file, either a video or a PQ still (PNG, HEIF or AVIF).

---
title: "A project's dynamic range"
description: "Choose whether a project works in SDR or HDR (HLG), and see what the switch does to your footage, titles, grades, keys and qualifiers."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

A project works in SDR or in HDR. The choice sets the colour every source is converted into, and which exports can carry HDR.

<AtAGlance
  where={['Document tab ▸ Canvas ▸ Dynamic Range', 'Document tab ▸ Document ▸ Colour']}
  tools={['set_canvas', 'get_project']}
/>

<Shot
  name="11-document-inspector.inspector"
  alt="The Document tab. The Document section's Colour row reads SDR — Rec. 709, and the Canvas section has a Dynamic Range popup set to SDR, above a Blending popup set to Encoded."
/>

## Choose SDR or HDR

<Steps>

1. Open the **Document** tab.

2. In the **Canvas** section, choose from the **Dynamic Range** popup.

</Steps>

| Item | What the project works in | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SDR** | Rec. 709 | Yes |
| **HDR (HLG)** | Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 | |

Switching is one undo step, **Dynamic Range**, and it changes no clip and no grade value. Choosing the item already showing changes nothing and makes no undo step.

The setting belongs to the whole project, so it works the same with a [nest](/editing/nests/) open. A new project starts as SDR.

## The Colour row

The **Document** section at the top of the tab shows your choice in its **Colour** row. It reads "SDR — Rec. 709" or "HDR — Rec. 2100 HLG".

## The HDR working space

An HDR (HLG) project composes every frame in HLG-encoded BT.2020, so HDR footage keeps its range all the way through to the file.

- An iPhone HDR clip keeps its highlights above white. HLG footage over BT.2020 passes through unchanged.
- PQ footage becomes real HDR, up to 1,000 cd/m². Brighter highlights are rolled off to fit, by the file's [peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/).
- Footage with a built-in [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) curve becomes real HDR.
- Frames are labelled BT.2100 HLG, and the 10-bit exports are tagged HLG.

In an SDR project the same HDR sources are converted to Rec. 709 instead, with their highlights rolled off. [How sources are read](/hdr/how-sources-are-read/) has the full table, HDR stills included.

## SDR material in an HDR project

SDR material is lifted so its white sits at HDR reference white. It looks as it did, and HDR highlights rise above it.

That covers BT.709 or untagged video, stills and screen recordings. Wide-gamut SDR footage is converted into BT.2020 and lifted the same way.

White is fixed at 203 cd/m² (HLG 75 %). There's no setting for the reference white.

## Drawn layers

Everything Frame Job draws is drawn as it is in SDR, then lifted to HDR reference white. That means text, captions, burn-in timecode, shapes, stills, graphics, and the background and shadow colours.

So a white title sits at reference white, not in the highlights, and a white graphic matches SDR white. Text, captions, shapes and graphics stay 8-bit even though they're lifted. See [Precision and bit depth](/hdr/precision/).

## Grades across a switch

Switching changes no grade value. The numbers stay as you set them, and the grade then runs on the project's working colour, with BT.2020's weights in an HDR (HLG) project.

A `.cube` look still reads its values as Rec. 709. In an HDR project the [Look section](/color/looks/) warns: "This project is HDR (HLG): a .cube LUT reads its values as Rec. 709."

## The chroma key across a switch

A [chroma key](/effects/chroma-key/) keeps keying the colour it was picked on. In an HDR (HLG) project it compares the colour an SDR project would show for each pixel, whether the layer is HLG, PQ, camera log or SDR, so it cuts the same pixels after the switch or very nearly.

| The key is | Layers |
| --- | --- |
| Exact | HLG footage over BT.2020, PQ up to 1,000 cd/m², footage with a built-in Camera Log except at its very brightest highlights, and SDR material |
| Close, not exact | HLG footage over P3 or BT.709 primaries, PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m², and a key picked on a gain-map photo |

Re-pick the key if an edge changes.

The eyedropper works to the same rule. In an HDR project it stores the picked colour as an SDR project shows it, so a key picked there means the same thing in either dynamic range.

## Qualifiers across a switch

A [qualifier](/color/qualifiers/) on an adjustment clip doesn't get that treatment. Its ranges are measured on the HLG values in an HDR (HLG) project, so re-pick them after switching. [Pick from Canvas](/color/pick-from-canvas/) reads an HDR frame at its HLG values.

## Exports and saved frames

An HDR (HLG) project can export an HLG master, an HDR10 file or an SDR version. [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/) says which formats write which.

**File ▸ Save Frame…** writes a 16-bit PNG or a 10-bit HEIC labelled BT.2100 HLG, and a JPEG writes the SDR version. See [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).

To see the SDR version before you export, turn on [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/). [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/) covers how the scopes read the picture.

## Good to know

- Wide-gamut SDR projects aren't offered. An SDR project always works in Rec. 709.
- There's no Dolby Vision output.
- How layers blend is a separate choice, right below this one. See [Blending](/hdr/blending/).

## With an agent

`set_canvas` switches the dynamic range. `new_project` has no option for it, so an agent sets it after making the project. Unlike the popup, `set_canvas` won't run inside a nest. See [Tools: tracks, markers and canvas](/mcp/tools-tracks-and-markers/).

## Related

- [How sources are read](/hdr/how-sources-are-read/)
- [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/)
- [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/)
- [The Document tab](/projects/document-tab/)
